title: Qwen3-VL
body_text: Qwen3-VL , the most powerful vision language model in the Qwen series is now available on Ollama’s cloud. The models will be made available locally soon. Model capabilities Visual Agent : Operates PC/mobile GUIs—recognizes elements, understands functions, invokes tools, completes tasks Visual Coding Boost : Generates Draw.io/HTML/CSS/JS from images/videos Advanced Spatial Perception : Judges object positions, viewpoints, and occlusions; provides stronger 2D grounding and enables 3D grounding for spatial reasoning and embodied AI Long Context & Video Understanding : Native 256K context, expandable to 1M; handles books and hours-long video with full recall and second-level indexing Enhanced Multimodal Reasoning : Excels in STEM/Math—causal analysis and logical, evidence-based answers Upgraded Visual Recognition : Broader, higher-quality pre-training is able to recognize everything more types of objects—celebrities, anime, products, landmarks, flora/fauna, etc Expanded OCR : Supports 32 languages (up from 19); robust in low light, blur, and tilt; better with rare/ancient characters and jargon; improved long-document structure parsing Text Understanding on par with pure LLMs : Seamless text–vision fusion for lossless, unified comprehension Get started Download Ollama Run the model ollama run qwen3-vl:235b-cloud Prompt the model with a message and image path(s). It is possible to use multiple images and drag and drop in images to make it easier to automatically type the file path. Examples Flower identification Prompt: What is this flower? Is it poisonous to cats? Menu understanding and translation Prompt: Show me the menu in English! Basic linear algebra Prompt: what’s the answer? Using Qwen3-VL 235B You can use Ollama’s cloud for free to get started with the full model using Ollama’s CLI, API, and JavaScript / Python libraries. JavaScript Library Install Ollama’s JavaScript library npm i ollama Pull the model ollama pull qwen3-vl:235b-cloud Example non-streaming output with image import ollama from 'ollama' const response = await ollama.chat({ model: 'qwen3-vl:235b-cloud', messages: [{ role: 'user', content: 'What is this?', images: ['./image.jpg'] }], }) console.log(response.message.content) Example streaming the output with image import ollama from 'ollama' const message = { role: 'user', content: 'What is this?', images: ['./image.jpg'] } const response = await ollama.chat({ model: 'qwen3-vl:235b-cloud', messages: [message], stream: true, }) for await (const part of response) { process.stdout.write(part.message.content) } Ollama’s JavaScript library page on GitHub has more examples and API documentation. Python Library Install Ollama’s Python library pip install ollama Pull the model ollama pull qwen3-vl:235b-cloud Example non-streaming output with image from ollama import chat from ollama import ChatResponse response: ChatResponse = chat( model='qwen3-vl:235b-cloud', messages=[ { 'role': 'user', 'content': 'What is this?', 'images': ['./image.jpg'] }, ]) print(response['message']['content']) # or access fields directly from the response object print(response.message.content) Example streaming the output with image from ollama import chat stream = chat( model='qwen3-vl:235b-cloud', messages=[{ 'role': 'user', 'content': 'What is this?', 'images': ['./image.jpg'] }], stream=True, ) for chunk in stream: print(chunk['message']['content'], end='', flush=True) Ollama’s Python library page on GitHub has more examples and API documentation. API The model can also be accessed directly on ollama.com’s API. Generate an API key from Ollama. Set OLLAMA_API_KEY environment variable using your API key. export OLLAMA_API_KEY=your_api_key Generate a response using API examples . OpenAI Compatible API Ollama has OpenAI compatible API endpoints that support the chat completions endpoint, completions endpoint, and the embeddings endpoint. Generate an API key from Ollama. The base_url should be set to https://ollama.com/v1 and api_key set to the one generated from above.

title: 3 ways to make a collage on iPhone
summary: Level up your photos! Learn how to make a collage on iPhone with free apps and built-in features that let you choose layouts and edit pics.
body_text: An image is worth a thousand words, sure. But a collage of images takes visual communication to a whole new level. They let you share multiple images at once, creating a story that evokes emotion, delivers a message, engages the audience, and makes your content memorable. A photo collage is an ideal visual tool in everything from social media posts to product advertisements to business presentations. One company that I worked for, in fact, asked new hires to create a collage of their interests, personality, experiences, and values to share with the team before their first day. This was a hugely effective way for new hires to communicate with their new co-workers, and to share the story of who they are. The value and appeal of a photo collage is clear. And with today’s technology and devices, it’s never been easier to create one. This article will focus on how to make a collage on an iPhone, profiling three tools that you can start using today. Table of contents: 5 reasons to make a collage on an iPhone 3 ways to create collages on your iPhone Build collages in minutes with Photoroom 5 reasons to make a collage on iPhone Let’s talk about some of the main reasons you might want to create a collage. Here are five, but I’m sure there are dozens more. Collages, after all, are super fun to make and share. 1. To share memories. Collages let you group together multiple photos from a special event—like a wedding, vacation, or birthday—or from a specific time period—such as an annual roundup or summer vacation throwback. They create visual stories that capture the essence of the occasion or period in time, allowing you to share the feeling and excitement with your friends, and look back fondly in future years. 2. To tell a story Storytelling, as mentioned above, is a big reason why collages are so popular. They’re an incredibly effective way to tell a comprehensive story—whether it’s about a specific event, an issue you’re discussing, or even about how certain objects or products relate to each other. By placing images alongside each other in a collage format, you create relationships between them, helping people understand how the story fits together. 3. To make a presentation pop Collages can play an important role in the business world too. Let’s face it: PowerPoint presentations are boring . Any way that you can spruce up your presentations a bit to make them any less boring is greatly appreciated amongst your audience. Collages add visual intrigue and storytelling to your presentation. They also allow you to get your point across faster, and in a more memorable way. A project manager, for example, might use a collage to illustrate key milestones and team efforts during a product launch to highlight key areas of focus for the team, and to ensure everyone understands the big picture quickly. 4. To showcase products online Ecommerce shops can also use collages to their advantage. This visual technique lets you display multiple angles or variations of your product in a single image, helping customers quickly understand the potential purchase. Even better, you can create collages of related products to quickly show customers how one item they like fits into a larger set of items. This can help to promote cross-selling and upselling at checkout. 5. As a creative outlet Lastly, many people use collages as a form of creative and artistic expression. The format allows you to experiment with different layouts, themes, and design elements, opening up a world of possibilities for how you present and arrange ideas visually. This is a particularly appealing artform for hobbyists, artists, and social media influencers who need a unique and engaging layout for their content. Being able to accomplish all of this on an iPhone, of course, is just icing on the cake. First off, it’s almost always on-hand. You don’t need to stop and use other devices outside of your daily flow. And modern apps—both built-in and third party—make it incredibly easy to create collages on an iPhone in a matter of seconds. iPhones also, of course, have incredibly high quality cameras that are extendable and customizable to the level of many professional devices. You can snap super high quality photos, edit them, and arrange them in a collage all on a single device. Add in the advanced editing features available through native and third-party apps, and you have a full-blown collage-generating machine in your pocket. 3 ways to create a collage on your iPhone There are literally dozens (maybe hundreds) of apps that will help you create a collage on your iPhone. For the sake of time, we’ve highlighted three in this article. 1. Shortcuts Let’s start with an app that’s built right into your iPhone. Shortcuts allows you to create personal shortcuts with multiple steps from your favorite apps. One of these shortcuts is called “Photo Grid,” which allows you to automate the process of creating a collage. Here’s how to get it. Open the shortcut app on your iPhone Navigate over to the “Gallery” tab at the bottom of the screen Search for “Photo Grid” and tap on it Tap “Add Shortcut” to add this automation to your collection of shortcuts Once loaded onto your iPhone, you can use the Photo Grid shortcut to create collages at any time, without the need to download or open a third-party app. Here’s how to create a collage: Go back to the “My Shortcuts” tab and find the “Photo Grid” shortcut you just added Tap on the shortcut to run it You’ll be prompted to select the photos you want to add to the collage Choose all photos from your camera roll by tapping on each one (you’ll see a checkmark in the top right corner of each thumbnail as you select them) Save your selections Once you’ve selected your images and hit save, the shortcut will automatically arrange the selected photos into a grid format, creating a collage. You can customize the layout, format, and arrangement of the collage by using the presets available to you in the app. Once you’re done, save the image to your camera roll and share it directly to various apps and platforms. 2. Photoroom Photoroom is a third-party app for iPhone users that is purpose-built to help users create stunning visuals on their phones or desktops. This includes creating photo collages, both through pre-made collage templates and with highly customizable drag-and-drop functionality. Photoroom is an excellent choice for creating high-quality collages on an iPhone, offering robust tools and customization options that cater to both casual users and professionals. Here’s how it works. First, download the Photoroom iOS app from the App Store, and install it on your phone. Launch the app, and start a new product. You have two options. Option 1: Start from photo Tap “Start from Photo” to add a new photo to your canvas This allows you select a photo from your camera reel Photoroom will automatically remove the background and give you the option of generating a new one—either from presets or from AI generated backgrounds You can also choose to preserve the original background from your photo if you prefer To start adding to your collage, tap “Insert” at the the bottom of your screen to add more photos to the design Again, Photoroom will remove the background for these new images and drop them into your canvas Repeat this process for each additional image you want to add Tap, drag, and resize your images to position them in the correct spot on the canvas You can also add text, apply filters, add stickers, and user other manual editing tools to customize the collage to your needs Click the image above to watch a video walkthrough of this process. Option 2: Start from template Scroll down on the main Photoroom screen until you see the “Collage” preset templates Select a template that matches your needs This will take you to the editing window where you’ll see placeholder images Click on the image icon for over each placeholder image, and select a new one from your camera roll. You can rearrange the template to your will, and add as many additional photos as needed Alternatively, you can also replace the image placeholders with shapes, graphics, stickers, logos, and more Use your fingers to adjust the size, placement, and angle of the images on the canvas If your template has text, tap on it and click the pencil icon to edit Like with the first option, you can also use Photoroom’s built-in editing features to add a wide range of customizations to the canvas Once you’re satisfied with your collage, tap “Export” to save it to your camera roll or share it directly via social media, email, or other platforms. Enhance your images effortlessly with our Photo Editor tools — powerful tools designed to make editing fast and intuitive. Perfect your photos with just a few clicks! 3. Google Photos app Google Photos is our third option. You likely know that it’s a photo management app, but did you also know that it has a collage-making feature that’s available for iPhone users? Here’s how it works. Download and install Google Photos from the App Store Launch the app on your phone, and sign in to your Google account to access your photos. Note: You can also sign up for a Google account and upload your camera photos to Google Photos. Tap on the “Library” tab at the bottom of the screen. Navigate to the “Utilities” section and tap on that. Under “Create New,” tap on “Collage” Select 2-9 photos from your photo reel that you want to include Once selected, tap “Create” Google will automatically arrange the selected photos into a collage You can then make basic adjustments to your collage by tapping on the edit icon Once you’re happy, tap “Save” to store your new collage in Google Photos. You can also share it directly from the app through various platforms like email, social media, or messaging apps. body_text: WESTMINSTER, Colo.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Jul. 29, 2026-- TriSalus Life Sciences® Inc. (Nasdaq: TLSI) (“TriSalus” or the “Company”), an oncology company integrating novel delivery technology with standard of care therapies to transform treatment for patients with solid tumors, today announced that Mary Szela, Chief Executive Officer and President, and David Patience, Chief Financial Officer, will participate in the Canaccord Genuity 46th Annual Growth Conference. Management will participate in one-on-one meetings on Tuesday, August 11 and Wednesday, August 12, and participate in a fireside chat on Wednesday, August 12 at 8:30 a.m. ET. A webcast replay of the corporate overview will be available for 90 days following the presentation in the Events section of the TriSalus Investor website at www.investors.trisaluslifesci.com . About TriSalus Life Sciences TriSalus Life Sciences® is an oncology focused medical technology company seeking to transform outcomes for patients with solid tumors by integrating its innovative delivery technology with standard-of-care therapies. The Company’s platform includes devices that utilize a proprietary drug delivery technology and a clinical stage investigational immunotherapy, nelitolimod, a class C Toll-like receptor 9 agonist, for a range of different therapeutic and technology applications. The Company’s two FDA-cleared devices use its proprietary Pressure-Enabled Drug Delivery™ (PEDD) approach to deliver a range of therapeutics: the TriNav® Infusion System for hepatic arterial infusion of liver tumors and the Pancreatic Retrograde Venous Infusion System for pancreatic tumors. The PEDD technology is a novel delivery approach designed to address the anatomic limitations of arterial infusion for the pancreas. The PEDD approach modulates pressure and flow in a manner that delivers more therapeutic to the tumor and is designed to reduce undesired delivery to normal tissue, bringing the potential to improve patient outcomes. Nelitolimod, the Company’s investigational immunotherapeutic candidate, is designed to treat the immunosuppressive environment created by many tumors and which can make current immunotherapies ineffective in the liver and pancreas. The Company is in the final stages of data completion for a number of phase 1 clinical trials and will begin exploring partnership opportunities for development. In partnership with leading cancer centers across the country – and by leveraging deep immuno-oncology expertise and inventive technology development – TriSalus is committed to advancing innovation that improves outcomes for patients. Learn more at trisaluslifesci.com and follow us on X (formerly Twitter) and LinkedIn . body_text: BWXT Completes Acquisition of Precision Components Group, Expanding U.S. Nuclear Manufacturing Capacity July 6, 2026 PDF Version LYNCHBURG, Va.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Jul. 6, 2026-- BWX Technologies, Inc. (NYSE: BWXT) announced today that it has successfully completed its previously announced acquisition of Precision Components Group, LLC (PCG), including its subsidiaries Precision Custom Components (PCC) and DC Fabricators (DCF). PCG is a U.S. manufacturer of complex, heavy-walled and heat-transfer components. The acquisition expands BWXT’s heavy-manufacturing footprint and enhances the company’s ability to deliver U.S.-made nuclear components for the commercial sector. “Growing demand for reliable, carbon-free energy underscores the urgent need to strengthen the U.S. nuclear manufacturing base,” said John MacQuarrie, BWXT president for Commercial Operations. “By expanding our manufacturing capabilities, we can better support reactor life-extension programs, new build activity and the long-term energy reliability our communities depend on.” PCG joins BWXT’s Commercial Operations segment and will continue operating at its current facilities in York, Pennsylvania, and Florence, New Jersey. The acquisition adds more than 500,000 square feet of U.S. heavy-manufacturing capacity, including large-envelope machining, heavy weldments, pressure vessels, heat exchangers and ASME-certified component fabrication, and a skilled workforce of over 450 employees. In addition to expanding commercial nuclear capacity, PCG will continue supporting existing workscopes, including components and services for Electric Boat, Bechtel Plant Machinery, Inc. and other U.S. Navy programs. title: Government Contracting BOE: How to Write One That Wins (July 2026)
summary: Winning government contracts in July 2026 starts with a solid BOE. Learn how to document labor, rates, and assumptions that hold up under DCAA review.
body_text: Your BOE can have the right numbers and still lose you points if evaluators can't trace the logic. Contracting officers and cost analysts read your BOE alongside your technical volume, and when those two documents tell different stories about staffing levels or task durations, that gap becomes a scoring risk. Building a BOE that actually wins means making sure every cost element connects back to something verifiable. TL;DR: A BOE documents how you priced every cost element and gives agencies a way to verify your estimate connects to actual PWS requirements. Cost-reimbursable and T&M contracts almost always require a BOE; sole-source awards above $2.5 million require certified cost or pricing data where a BOE is the primary vehicle. Your BOE must match your technical volume exactly: mismatched staffing levels, task durations, or missing cost lines are scored as proposal weaknesses. DCAA auditors trace every labor hour back to the SOW; unsupported round numbers, prior-year indirect rates, and pass-through subcontractor lines trigger formal findings. GovDash connects solicitation requirements to your cost structure by having Dash read the PWS, extract each requirement, and map it against your defined LCATs and Data Library rates. What a Basis of Estimate Is in Government Contracting A basis of estimate is a documented explanation of how a contractor arrived at its proposed costs. It breaks down the labor hours, materials, subcontractor costs, and other direct expenses tied to a specific scope of work, and explains the reasoning behind each figure. In government contracting, a BOE goes beyond a simple price breakdown. Agencies use it to assess whether a contractor truly understands the work, whether the proposed resources are realistic, and whether the numbers can be traced back to a defensible methodology. Why Agencies Care So Much About the BOE Contracting officers and cost analysts are doing more than checking math. They are asking whether the contractor's approach to scoping the work reflects the actual requirements in the PWS or SOW. A BOE that cannot answer that question clearly raises flags during source selection or cost/price analysis. The document serves a few interconnected purposes: It ties proposed costs directly to technical requirements, so reviewers can see that each labor category and hour estimate connects to a specific deliverable or task. It creates a paper trail that supports audit by DCAA or other oversight bodies, particularly on cost-reimbursable contracts where actual costs will be compared against the proposal. It protects the contractor during contract execution by documenting what was priced, preventing scope creep from being absorbed without a contract modification. A BOE is not optional on most competitive federal procurements. RFPs for cost-type contracts, IDIQ task orders , and many firm-fixed-price awards above simplified acquisition thresholds will include explicit instructions for submitting cost or pricing data along with supporting rationale. When a BOE Is Required Not every proposal requires a standalone BOE document, but contracting officers increasingly expect one whenever cost justification is non-trivial. Here is where a BOE is typically required or strongly expected: Cost-reimbursement contracts ( CPFF , CPAF, CPIF) almost always require a BOE because the government bears cost risk and needs to see how each labor category, material, and indirect cost rate was calculated before agreeing to fund the work. Time-and-materials contracts require a BOE tied to each LCAT, since the hourly rates and estimated hours drive the total contract value and must be defensible against wage determinations and market data. Large competitive acquisitions above the simplified acquisition threshold ($250,000 under FAR 2.101 ) routinely require a BOE as part of the pricing volume, especially when Section L includes explicit cost narrative instructions. Sole-source negotiations under FAR 15.403-4 require certified cost or pricing data when the contract exceeds the Truth in Negotiations Act threshold (currently $2.5 million for contracts awarded on or after July 1, 2018, per the October 2025 threshold adjustment), and a BOE is the primary mechanism for presenting that data. Even on fixed-price bids where a BOE is not formally required, a well-constructed one protects the contractor internally by documenting the assumptions behind the price and giving the team a reference point if the scope changes after award. Core Components of Every BOE Every BOE submitted to a government agency follows a predictable structure. Evaluators expect to see the same core elements, and missing any one of them raises questions about your team's ability to manage the work. The sections below cover what belongs in a complete BOE and what each one needs to contain. Scope Summary This section ties your estimate to a specific, bounded body of work. It should reference the relevant PWS or SOW paragraphs, name the deliverables, and call out any assumptions about what is and is not included. Undefined scope boundaries are one of the most common sources of later disputes, so being precise here protects both parties. Labor Estimation Labor is typically the largest cost driver, so this section receives the most scrutiny. For each labor category, you need to document the hours, the rationale behind those hours, and the basis for your loaded rates. If you are drawing rates from a GSA schedule, a CBA, or your approved forward pricing rate agreement, name the source explicitly. Applying a rate from an earlier fiscal year when a newer rate agreement is in place is the kind of error that can unravel an otherwise solid estimate. Materials and Other Direct Costs List each material or ODC line item separately. Generic placeholders like "miscellaneous supplies" are a red flag to evaluators. Each item should have a quantity, a unit cost, and a citation to the vendor quote or catalog that supports the figure. Indirect Costs and Fee Fringe, overhead, and G&A , and fee should be applied in the correct sequence and at the rates your accounting system actually uses. Pulling rates from a prior year's incurred cost submission instead of your current forward pricing agreement is a common error that DCAA auditors will flag. Assumptions and Exclusions Document every assumption that underlies the estimate. If the government's technical approach changes and your assumptions no longer hold, this section is what supports a contract modification. Unstated assumptions become scope disputes. BOE Estimation Methodologies Government contractors rely on several accepted methodologies when building a BOE, and the choice of approach shapes how well your estimate holds up under scrutiny. Common BOE Estimation Approaches There are four methods that appear most frequently in federal cost proposals: Method How It Works When to Use Best For Analogous Draws on actuals from a prior contract with similar scope, then adjusts for differences in complexity, size, or performance environment. Historical data is reliable and the new work closely mirrors a past contract. Familiar scope with well-documented past performance. Parametric Applies statistical relationships between cost drivers and outputs, such as lines of code per labor hour or square footage per installation day. Reliable productivity rates exist and input variables tie to verifiable data sources. Well-understood scope with quantifiable productivity metrics. Engineering (Bottom-Up) Builds cost from individual work packages, summing labor categories, hours, materials, and subcontract costs at the task level. Scope is distinct enough that historical comparisons would require heavy adjustment. Complex, performance-based contracts where detailed justification is required. Expert Judgment Relies on assessments from subject matter experts with direct experience in the relevant technical domain. Historical data is sparse or the work involves novel technical approaches. Filling estimation gaps where data is thin, with documented expert rationale. Choosing the Right Method Most winning proposals combine methods. A program manager might use parametric rates for Phase 1 staffing and bottom-up estimating for Phase 2 hardware integration, with expert judgment filling gaps where data is thin. The key is making the rationale visible to the reviewer so the estimate reads as calculated, not guessed. How to Build a BOE: A Step-by-Step Process A solid BOE moves through several discrete stages, each building on the last. Rushing any one of them tends to surface problems during government review. Scope the Work Before You Estimate Anything Read the PWS, SOW, or SOO carefully before touching a spreadsheet. Pull every deliverable, milestone, reporting requirement, and performance standard. Map each one to a labor category or resource type. If you can't tie a line item back to a contract requirement, it shouldn't be in the estimate. Build Your WBS and Assign Labor Categories Break the scope into a work breakdown structure. Assign labor categories that match your approved job descriptions and, where applicable, your GSA or CIO-SP3 labor category definitions. Mis-mapping LCATs to tasks is one of the fastest ways to draw a deficiency finding. Estimate Hours Using a Defensible Method Choose your estimation approach based on what the data supports: Analogous estimation draws from past performance on similar contracts, adjusting for scope differences with documented rationale. Parametric estimation applies historical productivity rates, such as lines of code per developer hour or deliverables per analyst month, to the current scope. Engineering build-up estimates each task from first principles when no comparable history exists. Document which method you used and why. Undocumented assumptions are the primary failure point in government BOE reviews. Apply Rates and Indirect Costs Apply fully loaded labor rates that match your approved forward pricing rate agreement, CAS-compliant cost accounting structure, or GSA schedule rates. Indirect costs including fringe, overhead, G&A, and fee must be applied consistently across the cost structure. Inconsistencies between your BOE rates and your SF 1411 or pricing model will trigger clarification requests. Cross-Check Against the Evaluation Criteria Before submission, read Section M. Confirm your BOE covers every factor evaluators will score as part of your price to win strategy . If the RFP calls out staffing rationale or phased ramp-up plans, those must appear in your narrative, beyond the spreadsheet alone. Documenting Labor Costs in Your BOE Labor is almost always the largest cost element in a government contract BOE, and evaluators will review it closely. Getting this section right means more than listing headcount; it means showing your work in a way that holds up under audit. Start by identifying each labor category (LCAT) you plan to use. For each one, you need to document: The number of hours assigned, broken down by contract period if the effort spans multiple years The fully loaded labor rate, which should reflect your approved forward pricing rate agreement or, if one does not exist, your most recent incurred cost submission data The basis for the hour estimate, such as a historical project with comparable scope, a staffing model tied to specific deliverables, or a time study Avoid the common mistake of applying a single blended rate across all labor categories. Evaluators expect to see rates tied to specific LCATs, and a blended rate signals either a shortcut or a lack of cost accounting discipline. If your contract uses a Service Contract Act or Davis-Bacon wage determination, you must show that your rates meet or exceed the applicable wage floor for each LCAT in each place of performance. A rate that looks reasonable in one city may fall below the required minimum in another. Finally, document any escalation assumptions applied across multi-year periods of performance. The Bureau of Labor Statistics Employment Cost Index is a commonly accepted escalation reference, and citing it by name gives evaluators a verifiable anchor for your year-over-year rate increases. Stating Assumptions, Exclusions, and Risk Every BOE section carries assumptions and exclusions that define its scope boundaries. Stating these clearly protects your firm if the government later claims your cost estimate should have covered work you never priced. Assumptions Assumptions are the conditions your estimate depends on to be valid. A BOE built on unstated assumptions is a liability. List every one explicitly, including expected period of performance, government-furnished equipment availability, staffing classifications under the applicable wage determination, and whether award fees or incentive structures affect labor allocation. Exclusions Exclusions tell the contracting officer what your price does not cover. If travel beyond a defined radius, integration with a legacy system, or data migration is out of scope, say so. Leaving exclusions implicit invites disputes during execution when the CO reads the SOW more broadly than you intended. Risk Factors Flag any conditions that could shift the estimate materially. Supply chain volatility, uncertain government approval timelines, or dependencies on subcontractor performance are legitimate risk factors worth naming. Reviewers respect specificity here far more than a boilerplate disclaimer about "unforeseen circumstances." Aligning Your BOE with the Technical Volume A BOE that lives in isolation from your technical volume is a liability. Evaluators read both documents together, and when the labor categories, task descriptions, or period-of-performance assumptions in your BOE don't match what your technical approach promises, the disconnect raises immediate questions about whether your team actually understands the work. The alignment check runs in both directions. Your technical volume sets commitments around staffing, schedule, and deliverables. Your BOE has to reflect those commitments with specificity: the same LCATs your technical approach names, the same phasing your project plan shows, and the same assumptions your management approach rests on. If your technical volume promises a dedicated quality assurance lead in Phase 1, your BOE needs a line item for that role with hours and a rate, not a vague "QA support" entry buried in indirect costs. A few areas where misalignment commonly breaks down: Staffing levels that don't match the org chart in the technical volume, such as a BOE showing three analysts when the technical narrative describes a five-person team structure. Task durations that contradict the project schedule, where the BOE estimates 200 hours for a deliverable the technical volume places on a 30-day timeline with two staff assigned. Assumptions in the BOE that reference contract conditions the technical volume never mentions, leaving evaluators with no way to trace the logic. Missing cost lines for activities the technical volume explicitly commits to, like site visits, government-furnished equipment coordination, or a transition period. Before submission, run a structured cross-check: pull every staffing reference, deliverable, and milestone from the technical volume and verify each has a corresponding cost element in the BOE. Any gap is a scoring risk. Common BOE Mistakes That Weaken Proposals Every number in a BOE needs to hold up under review by someone who was not in the room when the estimate was built. The most common failures share one trait: they require the evaluator to accept the contractor's word without a verifiable anchor. These are the errors that most often cause that. "Based on experience" without a data reference is not a rationale. Replace it with a prior contract number, a specific productivity metric from a comparable effort, or a named time study. Generic experience language cannot be verified and signals a shortcut. Labor hours that are not tied to specific SOW tasks leave reviewers unable to trace the logic. Each LCAT estimate should map to a named deliverable or task area, not a general program phase. Escalation rates applied without a cited index, such as the BLS Employment Cost Index or a specific wage determination schedule, will draw scrutiny on any multi-year award where year-over-year cost growth needs to be supported by a named source. Subcontractor costs listed as a single pass-through line invite an immediate deficiency. Each subcontractor should support their scope with their own hours, rates, and cost element breakdown. Figures that do not match between the BOE narrative and the cost volume spreadsheet signal that no one ran a reconciliation pass before submission. Contracting officers will issue clarification requests, and in competitive source selections, that gap may already be scored. BOE assumptions that conflict with staffing levels or timelines already stated in the technical volume tell evaluators the proposal team worked in silos. A useful internal test: give the BOE to someone unfamiliar with the pursuit and ask them to trace any single line item back to its source without your help. If they cannot, the rationale is not complete. What DCAA Auditors Look for in a BOE When a DCAA auditor reviews a BOE, they are not skimming for general reasonableness. They are tracing every cost element back to a documented, defensible rationale. Understanding what they look for helps contractors build BOEs that hold up under scrutiny from the start. Auditors focus on a few core areas: Labor hour estimates must connect directly to the SOW. If you estimate 500 hours for systems integration, the BOE needs to show how you arrived at that number, whether through historical actuals, engineering judgment, or parametric modeling. Unsupported round numbers are a red flag. Indirect rates must match your approved forward pricing rate agreement or the rates submitted to the contracting officer. Pulling rates from a prior fiscal year without noting the discrepancy can trigger a formal finding. Direct costs beyond labor, including materials, travel, and subcontractor costs, need their own backup. A subcontractor quote should accompany any subcontractor line item; a travel estimate should reference the applicable GSA per diem rates from the Federal Travel Regulation. Escalation factors applied to out-year costs need a named source, such as the Bureau of Labor Statistics Employment Cost Index or published wage determination schedules. Common BOE Deficiencies That Lead to Audit Findings Knowing the failure modes makes them easier to avoid. The most frequent problems auditors cite include estimates with no traceability to the SOW, labor categories that do not match the work described, indirect rates applied inconsistently across cost elements, and missing documentation for sole-source or sole-justification assumptions. Each of these deficiencies can result in a cost questioned or disallowed, which means the contractor absorbs that cost instead of recovering it from the government. Final Thoughts on Basis of Estimate Best Practices for Federal Proposals A solid BOE protects your firm at proposal time, during contract execution, and through any audit that follows. The work of connecting each cost line to a specific requirement, a named source, and a documented assumption is what separates a defensible estimate from one that gets questioned or disallowed. Your BOE is a record of how your team thinks, and reviewers read it that way. FAQ What should a basis of estimate include for a government contract proposal? A complete basis of estimate for a government contract needs a scope summary tied to specific PWS or SOW paragraphs, labor hour estimates broken down by LCAT with a documented rationale for each, materials and ODC line items with vendor citations, indirect costs applied at your current forward pricing rates, and a clearly stated list of assumptions and exclusions. Missing any one of these sections raises questions during source selection or DCAA audit. The assumptions section in particular carries substantial weight: it defines what you priced and protects you if the government's requirements shift after award. How do I choose between analogous, parametric, and bottom-up estimating for a federal BOE? The right method depends on what your data supports. Use analogous estimating when you have past contracts with comparable scope and can document the differences in complexity or size. Parametric estimating works well when you have reliable productivity rates, such as deliverables per analyst month or lines of code per developer hour, that you can tie to verifiable sources. Engineering bottom-up is the most defensible choice for complex, performance-based contracts where the scope is distinct enough that historical comparisons would require heavy adjustment. Most winning proposals combine all three, using parametric rates for well-understood phases and bottom-up builds for novel or high-risk task areas, with expert judgment filling gaps where data is thin.
